2. Demand and Supply

Subject: MOC - economics

Navigation

  • ← Previous: Basics of Economy
  • Next: National Income →
  • Subject MOC: MOC - economics
  • Vault index: Index

Content

  • Problem of Central Economy is limitation of resources. Since resources like money, raw materials, labor, and time are finite, an economy cannot produce everything it desires.
  • When resources in an economy are limited, they can be used in different ways to produce various goods and services. Depending on how these resources are used, different combinations of goods and services can be created.
  • The production possibility of the economy refers to all the possible combinations of goods and services that an economy can produce using the available resources and current technology.

Production Possibility Curve

  • It is a graph that shows the different combinations of two goods or services that an economy can produce when all resources are used efficiently.
  • E.g. If a person has ₹6000, and they have two buying options: 6 pairs of shoes for ₹6000 and 6 pairs of jeans for ₹6000. Spending the entire amount on one product means buying 6 pairs of shoes with no money left for jeans, or buying 6 pairs of jeans with no money left for shoes.

Graph 1: Negative sloping/Downward sloping curve (concave at origin)

  • It is seen in case of inverse relationship.
  • If they want more shoes, they must give up some jeans and vice versa. This also illustrates inverse relationship means that as we spend more money on one product we have less money available for the other product due to limitation on budget.

At any point

  • On the curve: Full utilisation of resources
  • Down/under the curve: Under utilisation of resources
  • Up/Over the curve: Not achievable (due to limited resources)

Opportunity Cost

  • Opportunity cost means the value of what you give up when you choose one thing over another.
  • E.g. If a person has ₹6000 and can buy either a pair of jeans or a pair of shoes, choosing the jeans means they miss out on getting the shoes. The shoes are the opportunity cost.

Free Goods

  • They are the type of goods that have no opportunity cost, as they are readily available in nature and not scarce, meaning there is no need to sacrifice the production of another good to obtain them; examples include air and sunlight.

Utility

  • Utility refers to the satisfaction or benefit a person gets from consuming a good or service.
  • E.g. If you eat a meal when you're hungry, the enjoyment and relief you feel is the utility you receive from that meal.

Types of Utility

Cardinal UtilityOrdinal Utility
Benefit gained from consumption of certain resources is measured in numerical valueBenefit gained from consumption of certain resources that are not measurable in numerical value
It is a quantitative approachIt is a qualitative approach
It is less realisticIt is more realistic

Consumer's Indifference Curve

  • A consumer's indifference curve is a graph that shows different combinations of two goods that provide the consumer with the same level of satisfaction or happiness.
  • E.g. At point A, we have 1 units of food and 12 units of clothing and point B, we have 2 units of food and 6 units of clothing. Both points make one equally happy, so they lie on the same indifference curve.

Graph 2: A consumer's indifference curve (Convex at origin)

Marginal Utility

  • The additional satisfaction or benefit that a consumer derived from buying an additional unit of a commodity/service.

Utility Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility

  • The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that as a person consumes more units of a good, the additional satisfaction (utility) derived from each extra unit gradually decreases, assuming all other factors remain constant.
  • E.g. Jab tum pehla golgappa khate ho toh jo anand ki prapti hoti hai woh dusre golgappe main nahi hoti kyunki dhire dhire additional satisfaction (utility) kam hota jata hai.

DEMAND

  • The quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to buy at a particular price during a specific period of time (willingness + ability).

Graph 3: Demand curve (Negative Sloping Curve - Inverse Relation Between Price and Demand, 'Other factors remain constant' (Ceteris Paribus). E.g. Income.)

  • There is an inverse relationship between price and demand. When the price of a product increases, people tend to buy less of it and when the price decreases, people usually buy more of it. However, this is not always true, this is true only under given conditions:
  1. 1. When income is constant.
  2. 2. When price of other goods is constant.
  3. 3. When there is no change in preferences.

Movement and Shift in Demand Curve

  • Movement in demand curve happens when there is a change in price of the product.
  • Shift in demand curve occurs when factors other than price change, such as income, consumer preferences, or the price of related goods changes.

Complimentary Goods vs Substitute Goods

Substitute GoodsComplimentary Goods
They refer to those goods which can be used in place of one another to satisfy a particular wantThey refer to those goods which are used together to satisfy a particular want
They have a competitive demandThey have a joint demand
Price of one substitute good, has positive relationship with quantity demanded of another substitute goodPrice of one complementary good has a negative relationship with the quantity demanded of another complimentary good
E.g. Tea and Coffee, Coke and PepsiE.g. Tea and Sugar, Car and Petrol
  • Shift on the curve can occurs in rightward or leftward position.
  • Curve shift to the rightward occurs when demand increases
  • Curve shift to the leftward occurs when demand decreases

Law of Demand

  • Law of Demand: It is a fundamental principle which states that there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

Exceptions to Law of Demand

  • Giffen Goods: It is a type of inferior goods/non-luxurious goods where demand may increase when prices rise, due to the absence of better alternatives or limited purchasing power.
  • E.g. Increase in price of wheat
  • Veblen Goods: Veblen goods are luxury goods that have a direct relationship between price and demand. This means that the demand for Veblen goods increases as their price increases, which is the opposite of the law of demand.
  • E.g. iPhone, Mercedes

Effect of Income on Inferior Products

  • Inferior goods are products whose demand decreases when consumer income rises, and demand increases when income falls, as people switch to better alternatives.

SUPPLY

  • Supply is the amount of a product or service that is available for purchase or use.

Supply Curve

  • A supply curve is a graphical representation of the relationship between the price of a good or service and the quantity that producers are willing and able to supply in a given period of time.

Graph 4: Supply curve - Positive sloping curve is seen when there is a direct relation between price and quantity supplied. Producers produce more when they get better price for their product.

When things exists in Equilibrium

Graph 5: Supply-Demand curve at Equilibrium

  • Equilibrium shifts, if any of the factors shift.
  • If demand decreases, the curve shifts to the left while if the demand increases, the curve shifts to the right.

Price Elasticity

  • Price elasticity of demand measures how much the quantity demanded of a good or service changes in response to a change in its price.

e_d = % change in demand / % change in price

Perfectly Elastic Demand

  • In perfectly elastic demand, a small rise in price results in a fall in demand to zero, while a small fall in price causes an increase in demand to infinity. In such a case, the demand is perfectly elastic or e = ∞. E.g. Luxury products such as gold and cars.

Graph 6: Perfectly Elastic Demand curve (Horizontal Curve, e = ∞)

Relatively Elastic Demand

  • Relatively elastic demand is when a small change in price leads to a large change in the quantity demanded of a product or service. This means that consumers are sensitive to price changes.

Graph 7: Relatively Elastic Demand curve (Slight change in price result in high change in demand, e_d > 1)

Perfectly Inelastic Demand

  • Perfectly inelastic demand is when the demand for a product remains the same regardless of price changes. This means that the quantity demanded is fixed and does not change. E.g. Necessary goods (water, wheat and rice).

Graph 8: Perfectly Inelastic Demand curve (Vertical curve, e_d = 0 - No changes in quantity of product demanded when the price changes)

Relatively Inelastic Demand

  • Relatively inelastic demand is when the demand for a product changes in response to price, but the change is not proportional to the price change. This means that the price of a product changes more than the demand for that product.

Graph 9: Relatively Inelastic Demand curve (e_d < 1 - Changes in price causes relatively less change in quantity demand)

Income Elasticity

  • Income elasticity of demand measures the relationship between a change in the quantity demanded for a particular good and a change in real income.
  • For most goods, when income goes up, demand goes up. The demand curve shifts to the right, showing a positive relationship.
  • For inferior goods (like cheaper options), when income rises, demand goes down. When income drops, demand for these goods goes up. The demand curve moves in the opposite direction.

Graph 10: Income Elasticity Curve (Income Elastic, Income Inelastic, Positive Income Elastic, Negative Income Inelastic)

Cross-Price Elasticity

  • Cross-price elasticity is an economic measure of how a change in the price of one good affects the demand for another good.
  • E.g. If the price of Pepsi rises by 10% and Coke's demand increases by 5%.

Graph 11: Cross-Price Elasticity Curve - If Price of Y increases, Qty of Y decreases, and Qty of X decreases (since X and Y are consumed together).

TYPES OF MARKET

Monopoly

  • One seller controls the entire market.
  • No close substitutes for the product.
  • High barriers to entry.
  • E.g. Indian railways

Oligopoly

  • A few large firms dominate the market.
  • Products may be similar or differentiated.
  • Many buyers for one product.
  • No easy entry.
  • E.g. Telecom sector, laptop market

Monopolistic Competition

  • Many sellers and many buyers for a product.
  • Products are similar but not identical (differentiated).
  • Some control over price.
  • Easy entry and exit.
  • E.g. Toothpaste

Perfect Competition

  • Many buyers and sellers.
  • Products are identical (homogeneous).
  • No barriers to entry.
  • Price is determined by supply and demand.
  • E.g. Agriculture products

MACROECONOMIC CONCEPTS

Marginal Propensity to Consume

  • Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) refers to the portion of additional income that a person spends on consumption rather than saving. It measures how much consumption increases when income rises by one unit.
  • MPC is dependent on the income level as it may vary with the income levels (MPC is lower at higher income levels).

MPC = Change in Consumption (ΔC) / Change in Income (ΔY)

  • MPC value: 0-1
  • E.g. If income rises by Rs. 10,000 and spending increases by Rs. 1,000, then:

MPC = 1000 / 10000 = 0.1

  • A MPC indicates that people are more likely to spend a larger portion of their additional income, leading to a greater increase in overall expenditure in the economy.

Autonomous Expenditure

  • It is the spending that occurs regardless of the level of income in an economy. It is independent of income.

C = A + cY

  • A: Income-independent consumption
  • cY: Income-dependent consumption
  • c: Marginal propensity to consume
  • Y: Level of income
  • C: Total consumption

Savings = 1 - c

Expenditure = 1 / (1 - c)

  • There is an inverse relationship between expenditure and savings.
